# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall series.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall series)
B1. Non-detained docket: house line is "13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities" (ICE data).
B2. Federal sentencing: use the all-offense share, "more than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences". The fall series does not break out offense type.
B3. Approved sources for the fall series: ICE, USSC, GAO, Texas DPS, CIS.
B4. Source line for B1-B3 figures: "Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)".
B5. Appendix notes: source line only.
B6. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B4 for B1-B3; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 13 (Jul 2026) - format reference

## Executive summary
- ...
- ...
- ...

## 1. ...

## Recommendations
1. Congress should ...

Appendix A1. ... Source: U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Southwest Land Border Encounters, Jun 2026, https://www.cbp.gov/...

Trump, Vance Wrong About 'Illegal Immigrant Murderers' - FactCheck.org 

 Skip to main content 

 FactCheck .org ® 

 A Project of The Annenberg Public Policy Center 

 This article is available in both English and Español 
 English 
 Español 

 In campaign appearances over the weekend in the swing state of Pennsylvania, former President Donald Trump and his running mate, Sen. JD Vance, falsely accused Vice President Kamala Harris of letting more than 13,000 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States.

 It’s true that there were 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder, as of July 21, who were not being detained by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 

 But the “vast majority” of them entered the country prior to the Biden administration and had their custody status determined “long before this Administration,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement, noting that many were in prison. Also, the noncitizens include those who entered the country legally, such as green-card holders.

 Trump and Vance distorted the contents of a Sept. 25 letter that Patrick Lechleitner , the acting director of ICE, sent to Rep. Tony Gonzales . The Republican congressman had requested the number of noncitizens who had committed a crime but were not in ICE custody — a list known as the agency’s non-detained docket.

 Lechleitner’s response included a chart that showed there are 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder who were not being detained by ICE. Homeland Security later clarified in its statement that “many” are in prisons, although it did not tell us how many are incarcerated when we inquired.

 Gonzales posted Lechleitner’s letter to X on Sept. 27. The next day, Vance referenced the 13,099 murderers at a campaign event in Newtown, Pennsylvania , and Trump did the same in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin . A day later, Trump repeated the claim in Erie, Pennsylvania .

 Vance, Sept. 28: Do you know that there are 13,000 — I know some of you are nodding because some of you saw this — 13,000 illegal immigrant murderers in the United States of America right now. They’re in this country because Kamala Harris let them in this country. 

 Trump, Sept. 29: During her term, it’s not even believable, she let in 13,099 convicted murderers. Some of them had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven. One murdered six.

 In its statement, the Department of Homeland Security said data in Lechleitner’s letter had been “misinterpreted.”

 “The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this Administration,” the statement said. “It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners.”

 Similarly, Michelle Mittelstadt , director of communications for the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute, told us that people have been on the non-detained docket “for decades.”

 “There is a lot of confusion around the non-detained docket,” including “who is on it and how long they’ve been on it,” Mittelstadt said in an email. “This docket has grown under multiple administrations, including the Trump one. Significant numbers of people on the docket have been on it for decades.”

 For example, the ICE acting director said in his letter that there are 425,431 convicted criminals on the agency’s non-detained docket as of July 21. But, as Mittelstadt noted, ICE reported in a budget document “that there were 405,786 convicted criminal noncitizens on the non-detained docket in June 2021 – so the vast majority would have gotten on during the prior administrations as the Biden administration by then was just five months old.” The number of people on the docket has increased by nearly 5% in about three years.

 She also told us that “the non-detained docket includes not just unauthorized immigrants but green-card holders and noncitizens on long-term non-immigrant visas who have made themselves removable by virtue of a criminal conviction.”

 The ICE letter to Gonzales did show that, as of July 21, there were an additional 1,845 noncitizens on the non-detained docket who face murder charges. But, again, we don’t know when those 1,845 people entered the United States, how many of them may have entered illegally and when they committed their alleged crimes. We also do not know if they are being held by other local, state or federal law enforcement agencies. A Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond when we asked for such information.

 We asked the Trump campaign to respond to the evidence that contradicts its candidates’ claims that Harris let 13,099 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States. We also asked it to supply information about Trump’s claim that some of the 13,099 “had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven.” In response, Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s national press secretary, said Trump “will begin the largest mass deportation in history on day one.”

 Mittelstadt said some murderers and other criminals cannot be deported “because their country will not accept their return.” In addition, she said, a 2001 Supreme Court ruling generally bars ICE from detaining noncitizens for more than six months if they are unlikely to be deported. As a result, ICE says on its website that it “has been legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, including those with serious criminal convictions.”

{"path": "/workspace/out/brief.md", "content": "# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE told Congress that as of July 21, 2024, 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket. Every one of them is a person ICE has identified as a killer and is not holding, and DHS has never said how many are behind bars today and how many are living in American communities.
- More than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 were not U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Congress does not need new authority to fix this. It needs to fund detention for the criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, penalize jurisdictions that refuse detainers, expand 287(g) and require DHS to report every criminal alien it releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On Sept. 25, 2024, ICE answered a congressional inquiry with a number that should have ended the argument over whether interior enforcement is a public-safety issue. As of July 21, 2024, the agency's non-detained docket carried 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions. The docket is ICE's list of noncitizens it knows about who are in removal proceedings or under final orders and whom it is not detaining. Not one of the 13,099 was in ICE custody. Neither were 15,811 noncitizens convicted of sexual assault, 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses and 2,663 convicted of motor vehicle theft, out of 425,431 convicted criminals on the docket.

DHS responded by noting that the records reach back about four decades and across administrations of both parties, that many of the 13,099 are incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities, and that the docket includes lawful residents whose convictions made them removable. All of that is true, and none of it is reassuring. If the records go back 40 years, so does the failure. If many of these killers are in state prison, the operative question is what happens the day their sentences end, and whether ICE will be waiting. And if the department can say only that "many" are incarcerated, it is conceding that it cannot tell the public how many are not.

That is the scandal in the number. A government that can list 13,099 convicted killers and cannot say how many of them are in a cell today has a detention problem and an accounting problem in the same caseload. Congress is asked to fund the first and has so far declined to mandate the second.

These figures have names attached. Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered on Feb. 22, 2024, while running on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Her killer, Jose Antonio Ibarra, entered the country illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released pending immigration processing. In August 2023, New York police arrested him on charges of acting in a manner injurious to a child; ICE said he was released before a detainer could be issued. A Georgia judge convicted him in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole. Congress responded with the Laken Riley Act, the first bill signed into law in 2025, which requires detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary, assaulting a law enforcement officer and other serious crimes. A statute is a start. It is not a bed, a bus or a deportation flight.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The same picture appears at the other end of the pipeline. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reports that of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 21,304, or 34.7%, were not U.S. citizens. Nearly nine in 10 of them, 88.7%, were illegal aliens. Another 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable.

These are federal-court figures. They measure the federal docket, not crime in America at large, and they are best read as a gauge of how many removable criminals the federal system processes in a year and what happens to them afterward. The answer to the second half of that question is the problem.

The Government Accountability Office supplies the trend line. The number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, from roughly 29,500 to about 21,500, and noncitizens fell from 19% of the federal prison population at the end of 2018 to 15% at the end of 2022. Falling prosecution and incarceration counts are only good news if removal follows, and ICE has said it is legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, including some with serious criminal convictions, because the Supreme Court has generally barred detention beyond six months when removal is not reasonably foreseeable (Zadvydas v. Davis, 2001). A system that convicts, imprisons and then loses track of a removable alien has not protected anyone. It has scheduled the next offense.

## 3. State data: Texas

Washington is not the only place that counts. Texas is the state that records immigration status in its arrest and conviction records, which makes Texas Department of Public Safety data the best available state-level test of how illegal aliens compare with everyone else.

Analysts who use those data disagree about what they show, and readers should know that before they repeat either side. The Cato Institute's Alex Nowrasteh, working from DPS conviction records for 2013 through 2022, puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 for native-born Americans. The Center for Immigration Studies disputes Cato's population denominators and argues that illegal immigrants whom DPS identifies only after incarceration are left out of the count, which would push the illegal-immigrant rate above the native rate.

This brief's argument does not rest on resolving that dispute, and it does not try to. The honest reading of the Texas record is that it is contested. The honest reading of the federal record is that it is not: ICE has 13,099 homicide convictions on a docket of people it does not hold, and it cannot say how many are incarcerated. That fact does not depend on anyone's estimate of the illegal-immigrant population of Texas.

The Texas fight does yield one firm conclusion. No single state should be the country's only source of information about crime and immigration status, and the fact that two research organizations can reach opposite conclusions from the same records is the clearest available argument for a mandatory, standardized federal data set.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

A detainer is a request, on Form I-247, that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after he would otherwise be released, so that ICE can take him into custody. It is not a warrant, and jurisdictions that refuse to honor one know what follows. The arrest that could have been made in a booking room has to be made later, at large, by an agent who does not know whether the subject is armed, or it is not made at all.

Sanctuary policies are a policy choice, and Congress funds a great deal of what those policies cost the rest of the country. The Ibarra case is the standard illustration: a removable alien with a live criminal charge was released by a local agency, according to ICE, before the detainer could even be filed. Section 287(g) agreements are the proven alternative, allowing trained local officers to identify removable criminals inside the jail, where the encounter is cheapest and safest for everyone involved.

1. **Fund the criminal-alien docket.** Appropriate detention capacity and removal flights specifically against the non-detained docket's most serious conviction categories, beginning with homicide and sexual assault, and set a public annual target for the number of those cases moved off the docket.
2. **Mandate detainer compliance.** Condition federal law-enforcement assistance on honoring ICE detainers and on notifying ICE before a removable alien in local custody is released.
3. **Expand 287(g).** Fund enough training slots and reimbursement to approve every qualified jail-enforcement application from a state or locality that requests one.
4. **Require DHS reporting.** Direct quarterly publication of the non-detained docket by conviction category and current custody status, including how many people in each category are incarcerated by another authority and how many are not in any custody.
5. **Close the Zadvydas gap.** Provide explicit detention authority, with periodic judicial review, for removable aliens convicted of violent felonies whose countries refuse to accept their return.

Congress should make that a condition of the next appropriation, and should keep making it one until the number 13,099 starts going down for the right reason: because ICE is holding the people on that list, or because they have been removed.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary
- ICE told Congress that as of July 21, 2024, 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket. Every one of them is a person ICE has identified as a killer and is not holding, and DHS has never said how many are behind bars today and how many are living in American communities.
- More than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 were not U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Congress does not need new authority to fix this. It needs to fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, penalize jurisdictions that refuse detainers, expand 287(g) and require DHS to report every criminal alien it releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On Sept. 25, 2024, ICE answered a congressional inquiry with a number that should have ended the argument about whether interior enforcement is a public-safety issue. As of July 21, 2024, the agency's non-detained docket carried 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions. The docket is the list of noncitizens ICE knows about who are in removal proceedings or under final orders and whom the agency is not detaining. None of the 13,099 was in ICE custody. Neither were 15,811 noncitizens convicted of sexual assault, 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses and 2,663 convicted of motor vehicle theft, out of 425,431 convicted criminals on the docket.

DHS responded to the release of the number by pointing out that the records reach back four decades and across administrations of both parties, that many of the 13,099 are incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities, and that the docket includes lawful residents whose convictions made them removable. All of that is true, and none of it is reassuring. If the records go back 40 years, so does the failure. If many of these killers are in state prison, the operative question is what happens the day they finish their sentences, and whether ICE will be waiting. If the department can say only that "many" are incarcerated, it is conceding that it cannot tell the public how many are not.

That is the scandal in the number. A government that can list 13,099 convicted killers and cannot say how many are in a cell today has a detention problem and an accounting problem in the same caseload.

These figures have names attached. Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered on Feb. 22, 2024, while running on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Her killer, Jose Antonio Ibarra, entered the country illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released pending immigration processing. In August 2023, New York police arrested him on charges of acting in a manner injurious to a child; ICE said he was released before a detainer could be issued. A Georgia judge convicted him in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole. Congress answered with the Laken Riley Act, the first bill signed into law in 2025, which requires detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary, assaulting an officer and other serious crimes. A statute is a start. It is not a bed, a bus or a deportation flight.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The same picture appears at the other end of the pipeline. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reports that of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 21,304, or 34.7%, were not U.S. citizens. Nearly nine in 10 of them, 88.7%, were illegal aliens. Another 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable.

These are federal-court figures. They measure the federal docket, not crime in America at large, and they are best read as a gauge of how many removable criminals the federal system processes in a year and what happens to them afterward. [Hmm — this is where honesty matters. I'm flagging that they measure the federal docket, which prevents the false inference. Good.]

Falling prosecutions are only good news if removal follows. ICE has said that it is legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, including some with serious criminal convictions, because the Supreme Court has generally barred detention for more than six months when removal is not reasonably foreseeable (Zadvydas v. {"content": "# FACT SHEET: Criminal Aliens and Public Safety

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026
For Hill offices. Companion to "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy.

## The numbers

**13,099** noncitizens with homicide convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024. Not one of them was in ICE custody. DHS has said only that "many" are incarcerated by other authorities; it has never reported how many are in a cell and how many are in American communities.¹

**425,431** convicted criminals were on that same docket, including **15,811** noncitizens convicted of sexual assault, **13,423** convicted of weapons offenses and **2,663** convicted of motor vehicle theft.¹

**647,572** of the **662,556** noncitizens on ICE's docket with criminal convictions or pending charges were not in ICE detention.¹

**34.7%** of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 were not U.S. citizens: 21,304 of 61,342. These are federal-court figures; they measure the federal docket, not crime in the country at large.²

**88.7%** of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. Another 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable.²

**27%** fewer noncitizens were sentenced for federal crimes in fiscal 2023 than in fiscal 2018, down from about 29,500 to about 21,500.³

**15%** of the federal prison population was noncitizen at year-end 2022, down from 19% at year-end 2018. Declining prosecution and incarceration counts protect the public only if removal follows.³

## What Congress can do

- **Fund the criminal-alien docket.** Appropriate detention capacity and removal flights against the non-detained docket's most serious conviction categories, beginning with homicide and sexual assault, with a public annual target.
- **Mandate detainer compliance.** Condition federal law-enforcement assistance on honoring ICE detainers and on notifying ICE before a removable alien is released.
- **Expand 287(g).** Fund enough training slots to approve every qualified jail-enforcement application that requests one.
- **Require DHS reporting.** Direct quarterly publication of the non-detained docket by conviction category and current custody status, including how many are incarcerated by another authority and how many are not in any custody.
- **Close the *Zadvydas* gap.** Provide detention authority, with periodic judicial review, for removable aliens convicted of violent felonies whose countries refuse to accept their return.

The Laken Riley Act (Public Law 119-1, signed Jan. 29, 2025) already requires detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary, assaulting a law enforcement officer and other serious crimes.⁴ The mandate is on the books; the beds, the compliance and the reporting are not.

---

### Sources

1. Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).
2. Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).
3. U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations, Oct. 2024 (GAO-24-107598).
4. Public Law 119-1, Laken Riley Act, Jan. 29, 2025.

{"content": "**EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10:00 a.m. ET**
**Contact: Office of Communications, Founders' Square Institute, [media contact to be inserted before release]**

# Federal Data Show 13,099 Convicted Killers on ICE's Non-Detained Docket; DHS Cannot Say How Many Are Incarcerated

**WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026** — ICE reported to Congress that 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, and the Department of Homeland Security has never said how many of them are behind bars today and how many are living in American communities, the Founders' Square Institute said today.

The finding opens Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy. The brief asks Congress to fund detention for the criminal aliens on the docket, penalize jurisdictions that ignore ICE detainers, expand 287(g) agreements and require quarterly public reporting from DHS.

The same docket held 425,431 convicted criminals, including 15,811 noncitizens convicted of sexual assault and 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses. Of the 662,556 noncitizens on the docket with convictions or pending charges, 647,572 were outside ICE detention.

Federal sentencing data point the same way: more than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 were not U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of them were illegal aliens.

"The federal government can list 13,099 convicted killers and cannot tell the public how many are in a cell today," Kessler said. "That is a detention problem and an accounting problem in the same caseload, and Congress can fix both in the next appropriations bill. Fund the docket, enforce the detainers and make DHS report every criminal alien it releases."

The brief also finds that the only state-level data set that records immigration status, from Texas, is contested between researchers and argues that Congress should settle the question with a mandatory, standardized federal data set.

Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, the data appendix and a fact sheet for Hill offices are available at the FSI website.

**The Founders' Square Institute** is a Washington, D.C., public-policy think tank. FSI publications are drafts until approved by the Director of Publications.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE told Congress that as of July 21, 2024, 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket. Every one of them is a person ICE has identified as a killer and is not holding, and DHS has never said how many are behind bars today and how many are living in American communities.
- More than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 were not U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Congress does not need new authority to fix this. It needs to fund detention for the criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, penalize jurisdictions that refuse detainers, expand 287(g) and require DHS to report every criminal alien it releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On Sept. 25, 2024, ICE answered a congressional inquiry with a number that should have ended the argument over whether interior enforcement is a public-safety issue. As of July 21, 2024, the agency's non-detained docket carried 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions. The docket is ICE's list of noncitizens it knows about who are in removal proceedings or under final orders and whom it is not detaining. Not one of the 13,099 was in ICE custody. Neither were 15,811 noncitizens convicted of sexual assault, 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses and 2,663 convicted of motor vehicle theft, out of 425,431 convicted criminals on the docket.

DHS responded by noting that the records reach back about four decades and across administrations of both parties, that many of the 13,099 are incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities, and that the docket includes lawful residents whose convictions made them removable. All of that is true, and none of it is reassuring. If the records go back 40 years, so does the failure. If many of these killers are in state prison, the operative question is what happens the day their sentences end, and whether ICE will be waiting. And if the department can say only that "many" are incarcerated, it is conceding that it cannot tell the public how many are not.

That is the scandal in the number. A government that can list 13,099 convicted killers and cannot say how many of them are in a cell today has a detention problem and an accounting problem in the same caseload. Congress is asked to fund the first and has so far declined to mandate the second.

These figures have names attached. Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered on Feb. 22, 2024, while running on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Her killer, Jose Antonio Ibarra, entered the country illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released pending immigration processing. In August 2023, New York police arrested him on charges of acting in a manner injurious to a child; ICE said he was released before a detainer could be issued. A Georgia judge convicted him in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole. Congress responded with the Laken Riley Act, the first bill signed into law in 2025, which requires detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary, assaulting a law enforcement officer and other serious crimes. A statute is a start. It is not a bed, a bus or a deportation flight.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The same picture appears at the other end of the pipeline. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reports that of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 21,304, or 34.7%, were not U.S. citizens. Nearly nine in 10 of them, 88.7%, were illegal aliens. Another 8.5% were legal aliens.

These are federal-court figures. They measure the federal docket, not crime in America at large, and they are best read as a gauge of how many noncitizens the federal criminal system handles in a year and what happens to them afterward. The answer to the second half of that question is the problem.

The Government Accountability Office supplies the trend line. The number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, from roughly 29,500 to about 21,500, and noncitizens fell from 19% of the federal prison population at the end of 2018 to 15% at the end of 2022. Falling prosecution and incarceration counts are only good news if removal follows, and ICE has said it is legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, including some with serious criminal convictions, because the Supreme Court has generally barred detention beyond six months when removal is not reasonably foreseeable (Zadvydas v. Davis, 2001). A system that convicts, imprisons and then loses track of a removable alien has not protected anyone. It has scheduled the next offense.

## 3. State data: Texas

Washington is not the only place that counts. Texas is the state that records immigration status in its arrest and conviction records, which makes Texas Department of Public Safety data the best available state-level test of how illegal aliens compare with everyone else.

Analysts who use those data disagree about what they show, and readers should know that before they repeat either side. The Cato Institute's Alex Nowrasteh, working from DPS conviction records for 2013 through 2022, puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 for native-born Americans. The Center for Immigration Studies disputes Cato's population denominators and argues that illegal immigrants whom DPS identifies only after incarceration are left out of the count, which would push the illegal-immigrant rate above the native rate.

This brief's argument does not rest on resolving that dispute, and it does not try to. The honest reading of the Texas record is that it is contested. The honest reading of the federal record is that it is not: ICE has 13,099 homicide convictions on a docket of people it does not hold, and it cannot say how many are incarcerated. That fact does not depend on anyone's estimate of the illegal-immigrant population of Texas.

The Texas fight does yield one firm conclusion. No single state should be the country's only source of information about crime and immigration status, and the fact that two research organizations can reach opposite conclusions from the same records is the clearest available argument for a mandatory, standardized federal data set.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

A detainer is a request, on Form I-247, that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after he would otherwise be released, so that ICE can take him into custody. It is not a warrant, and jurisdictions that refuse to honor one know what follows. The arrest that could have been made in a booking room has to be made later, at large, by an agent who does not know whether the subject is armed, or it is not made at all.

Sanctuary policies are a policy choice, and Congress funds a great deal of what those policies cost the rest of the country. The Ibarra case is the standard illustration: a removable alien with a live criminal charge was released by a local agency, according to ICE, before the detainer could even be filed. Section 287(g) agreements are the proven alternative, allowing trained local officers to identify removable criminals inside the jail, where the encounter is cheapest and safest for everyone involved.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund the criminal-alien docket.** Appropriate detention capacity and removal flights specifically against the non-detained docket's most serious conviction categories, beginning with homicide and sexual assault, and set a public annual target for the number of those cases moved off the docket.
2. **Mandate detainer compliance.** Condition federal law-enforcement assistance on honoring ICE detainers and on notifying ICE before a removable alien in local custody is released.
3. **Expand 287(g).** Fund enough training slots and reimbursement to approve every qualified jail-enforcement application from a state or locality that requests one.
4. **Require DHS reporting.** Direct quarterly publication of the non-detained docket by conviction category and current custody status, including how many people in each category are incarcerated by another authority and how many are not in any custody.
5. **Close the Zadvydas gap.** Provide explicit detention authority, with periodic judicial review, for removable aliens convicted of violent felonies whose countries refuse to accept their return.

The federal government already collects the information that would tell the public how many convicted killers it is holding and how many it is not. It declines to publish it. Congress should make that a condition of the next appropriation, and should keep making it one until the number 13,099 starts going down for the right reason: because ICE is holding the people on that list, or because they have been removed.

The finding opens Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy. The brief asks Congress to fund detention for the criminal aliens on the docket, penalize jurisdictions that ignore ICE detainers, expand 287(g) agreements and require quarterly public reporting from DHS.

The same docket held 425,431 convicted criminals, including 15,811 noncitizens convicted of sexual assault and 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses. Of the 662,556 noncitizens on the docket with convictions or pending charges, 647,572 were outside ICE detention.

Federal sentencing data point the same way: more than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 were not U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of them were illegal aliens.

"The federal government can list 13,099 convicted killers and cannot tell the public how many are in a cell today," Kessler said. "That is a detention problem and an accounting problem in the same caseload, and Congress can fix both in the next appropriations bill. Fund the docket, enforce the detainers and make DHS report every criminal alien it releases."

The brief also finds that the only state-level data set that records immigration status, from Texas, is contested between researchers, and argues that Congress should settle the question with a mandatory, standardized federal data set.

Brief No. 14, the data appendix and a Hill fact sheet are available on the FSI website.

**The Founders' Square Institute** is a Washington, D.C., public-policy think tank.

# Data Appendix - Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

**Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show**
By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026

One table per figure used in the brief, the fact sheet, the press release and the stat cards. Source lines follow style sheet rev. 4 (B4-C1). Notes are source lines only, per B5.

---

## Table A1. ICE non-detained docket: convicted criminals, as of July 21, 2024

| Measure | Noncitizens |
|---|---|
| Convicted criminals on the non-detained docket | 425,431 |
| Of those, with homicide convictions | 13,099 |
| Of those, with sexual assault convictions | 15,811 |
| Of those, with weapons-offense convictions | 13,423 |
| Of those, with motor vehicle theft convictions | 2,663 |
| Noncitizens on the docket with homicide charges pending | 1,845 |
| Total noncitizens on the docket with convictions or pending charges | 662,556 |
| Of those, not in ICE detention | 647,572 |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).

---

## Table A2. Federal sentencing, fiscal 2024: citizenship of individuals sentenced

| Individuals sentenced in federal court, fiscal 2024 | Number | Share |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. citizens | 40,038 | 65.3% |
| Non-U.S. citizens | 21,304 | 34.7% |
| **Total** | **61,342** | **100.0%** |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).

---

## Table A3. Immigration status of the 21,304 non-U.S. citizens sentenced in federal court, fiscal 2024

| Status | Share of noncitizens sentenced |
|---|---|
| Illegal aliens | 88.7% |
| Legal aliens | 8.5% |
| Extradited aliens | 1.3% |
| Unknown status | 1.5% |
| **Total** | **100.0%** |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).

---

## Table A4. Noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes, fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2023

| Fiscal year | Noncitizens sentenced (approx.) |
|---|---|
| 2018 | 29,500 |
| 2023 | 21,500 |
| Change | down 27% |

Source: U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations, Oct. 2024 (GAO-24-107598).

---

## Table A5. Noncitizen share of the federal prison population, year-end 2018 and year-end 2022

| Year-end | Share of federal prison population |
|---|---|
| 2018 | 19% |
| 2022 | 15% |

Source: U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations, Oct. 2024 (GAO-24-107598).

---

## Table A6. Homicide conviction rates in Texas by immigration status, 2013-2022 (contested estimates; see Brief No. 14, Section 3)

| Group | Homicide convictions per 100,000, Texas, 2013-2022 |
|---|---|
| Illegal immigrants | 2.2 |
| Native-born Americans | 3.0 |
| Legal immigrants | 1.2 |

Source: Cato Institute, A. Nowrasteh, Illegal Immigrant Murderers in Texas, 2013-2022, Jun. 2024 (Texas Department of Public Safety conviction data).
Source: Center for Immigration Studies, J. Richwine, Misuse of Texas Data Understates Illegal Immigrant Criminality, Oct. 2022 (Texas Department of Public Safety data).

---

## Charts (production specifications, per style sheet B6)

Palette: FSI navy #1F3A5F (primary series), FSI red #B22234 (emphasis series). No third color. Bar charts run from zero. Trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

### Chart 1. ICE non-detained docket by conviction category, July 21, 2024
Type: vertical bar chart, bars run from zero, values labeled on each bar.
Emphasis bar (FSI red #B22234): Homicide, 13,099.
Standard bars (FSI navy #1F3A5F): Sexual assault, 15,811; Weapons offenses, 13,423; Motor vehicle theft, 2,663.
Title: "Convicted criminals on ICE's non-detained docket"
Source line under chart: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS).

### Chart 2. Noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes
Type: two-bar column chart, bars run from zero, values labeled.
FSI navy #1F3A5F: fiscal 2018, 29,500; fiscal 2023, 21,500.
Title: "Noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes, fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2023"
Source line under chart: U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations, Oct. 2024 (GAO-24-107598).
If the design team charts GAO's full fiscal 2018-2023 series as a line, start the y-axis at the series minimum per B6.

---

## Primary documents referenced in Brief No. 14

- ICE, letter from Patrick J. Lechleitner, acting director, to Rep. Tony Gonzales, Sept. 25, 2024 (data as of July 21, 2024).
- U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, Fiscal Year 2024.
- U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations, Oct. 2024 (GAO-24-107598).
- Texas Department of Public Safety, conviction and arrest data by immigration status, 2013-2022.
- Cato Institute, A. Nowrasteh, Illegal Immigrant Murderers in Texas, 2013-2022, Jun. 2024.
- Center for Immigration Studies, J. Richwine, Misuse of Texas Data Understates Illegal Immigrant Criminality, Oct. 2022.
- Public Law 119-1, Laken Riley Act, Jan. 29, 2025.
- Zadvydas v. Davis, 533 U.S. 678 (2001).

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE told Congress that as of July 21, 2024, 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket. Every one of them is a person ICE has identified as a killer and is not holding, and DHS has never said how many are behind bars today and how many are living in American communities.
- More than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 were not U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Congress does not need new authority to fix this. It needs to fund detention for the criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, penalize jurisdictions that refuse detainers, expand 287(g) and require DHS to report every criminal alien it releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On Sept. 25, 2024, ICE answered a congressional inquiry with a number that should have ended the argument over whether interior enforcement is a public-safety issue. As of July 21, 2024, the agency's non-detained docket carried 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions. The docket is ICE's list of noncitizens it knows about who are in removal proceedings or under final orders and whom it is not detaining. Not one of the 13,099 was in ICE custody. Neither were 15,811 noncitizens convicted of sexual assault, 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses and 2,663 convicted of motor vehicle theft, out of 425,431 convicted criminals on the docket.

DHS responded by noting that the records reach back about four decades and across administrations of both parties, that many people on the docket are incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities, and that the docket includes lawful residents whose convictions made them removable. All of that is true, and none of it is reassuring. If the records go back 40 years, so does the failure. If some of those killers are in state prison, the operative question is what happens the day their sentences end, and whether ICE will be waiting. And if the department can say only that "many" are incarcerated, it is conceding that it cannot tell the public how many are not.

That is the scandal in the number. A government that can list 13,099 convicted killers and cannot say how many of them are in a cell today has a detention problem and an accounting problem in the same caseload. Congress is asked to fund the first and has so far declined to mandate the second.

These figures have names attached. Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered on Feb. 22, 2024, while running on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Her killer, Jose Antonio Ibarra, entered the country illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released pending immigration processing. In August 2023, New York police arrested him on charges of acting in a manner injurious to a child; ICE said he was released before a detainer could be issued. A Georgia judge convicted him in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole. Congress responded with the Laken Riley Act, the first bill signed into law in 2025, which requires detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary, assaulting a law enforcement officer and other serious crimes. A statute is a start. It is not a bed, a bus or a deportation flight.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The same picture appears at the other end of the pipeline. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reports that of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 21,304, or 34.7%, were not U.S. citizens. Nearly nine in 10 of them, 88.7%, were illegal aliens. Another 8.5% were legal aliens.

These are federal-court figures. They measure the federal docket, not crime in America at large, and they are best read as a gauge of how many noncitizens the federal criminal system handles in a year. What happens to them afterward is where the system breaks.

The Government Accountability Office supplies the trend line. The number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, from roughly 29,500 to about 21,500, and noncitizens fell from 19% of the federal prison population at the end of 2018 to 15% at the end of 2022. Falling prosecution and incarceration counts are only good news if removal follows, and ICE has said it is legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, including some with serious criminal convictions, because the Supreme Court has generally barred detention beyond six months when removal is not reasonably foreseeable (Zadvydas v. Davis, 2001). A system that convicts, imprisons and then loses track of a removable alien has not protected anyone. It has scheduled the next offense.

## 3. State data: Texas

Washington is not the only place that counts. Texas has the most complete state record: its Department of Public Safety records immigration status in arrest and conviction data, which makes DPS numbers the best available state-level test of how illegal aliens compare with everyone else.

Analysts who use those data disagree about what they show, and readers should know that before they repeat either side. The Cato Institute's Alex Nowrasteh, working from DPS conviction records for 2013 through 2022, puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 for native-born Americans. The Center for Immigration Studies disputes Cato's population denominators and argues that illegal immigrants whom DPS identifies only after incarceration are left out of the count, which would push the illegal-immigrant rate above the native rate.

This brief's argument does not rest on resolving that dispute, and it does not try to. The honest reading of the Texas record is that it is contested. The honest reading of the federal record is that it is not: ICE has 13,099 homicide convictions on a docket of people it does not hold, and it cannot say how many are incarcerated. That fact does not depend on anyone's estimate of the illegal-immigrant population of Texas.

The Texas fight does yield one firm conclusion. No single state should be the country's only source of information about crime and immigration status, and the fact that two research organizations can reach opposite conclusions from the same records is the clearest available argument for a mandatory, standardized federal data set.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

A detainer is a request, on Form I-247, that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after he would otherwise be released, so that ICE can take him into custody. It is not a warrant, and jurisdictions that refuse to honor one know what follows. The arrest that could have been made in a booking room has to be made later, at large, by an agent who does not know whether the subject is armed, or it is not made at all.

Sanctuary policies are a policy choice, and Congress funds a great deal of what those policies cost the rest of the country. The Ibarra case is the standard illustration: a removable alien with a live criminal charge was released by a local agency, according to ICE, before the detainer could even be filed. The Laken Riley Act answered by requiring DHS to issue a detainer for anyone covered by its new mandatory-detention categories and by giving state attorneys general standing to sue the secretary when enforcement fails. Section 287(g) agreements are the other proven answer, allowing trained local officers to identify removable criminals inside the jail, where the encounter is cheapest and safest for everyone involved.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund the criminal-alien docket.** Appropriate detention capacity and removal flights specifically against the non-detained docket's most serious conviction categories, beginning with homicide and sexual assault, and set a public annual target for the number of those cases moved off the docket.
2. **Mandate detainer compliance.** Condition federal law-enforcement assistance on honoring ICE detainers and on notifying ICE before a removable alien in local custody is released.
3. **Expand 287(g).** Fund enough training slots and reimbursement to approve every qualified jail-enforcement application from a state or locality that requests one.
4. **Require DHS reporting.** Direct quarterly publication of the non-detained docket by conviction category and current custody status, including how many people in each category are incarcerated by another authority and how many are not in any custody.
5. **Close the Zadvydas gap.** Provide explicit detention authority, with periodic judicial review, for removable aliens convicted of violent felonies whose countries refuse to accept their return.

The federal government already collects the information that would tell the public how many convicted killers it is holding and how many it is not. It declines to publish it. Congress should make that a condition of the next appropriation, and should keep making it one until the number 13,099 starts going down for the right reason: because ICE is holding the people on that list, or because they have been removed.

**EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10:00 a.m. ET**
**Contact: Office of Communications, Founders' Square Institute, [media contact to be inserted before release]**

# Federal Data Show 13,099 Homicide Convictions on ICE's Non-Detained Docket

**WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026** — ICE reported to Congress that 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, and DHS has never said how many of them are behind bars today and how many are living in American communities, the Founders' Square Institute said today.

The finding opens Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy. The brief asks Congress to fund detention for the criminal aliens on the docket, penalize jurisdictions that ignore ICE detainers, expand 287(g) agreements and require quarterly public reporting from DHS.

The same docket held 425,431 convicted criminals, including 15,811 noncitizens convicted of sexual assault and 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses. Of the 662,556 noncitizens on the docket with convictions or pending charges, 647,572 were outside ICE detention.

Federal sentencing data point the same way: more than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 were not U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of them were illegal aliens.

"The federal government can list 13,099 convicted killers and cannot tell the public how many are in a cell today," Kessler said. "That is a detention problem and an accounting problem in the same caseload, and Congress can fix both in the next appropriations bill. Fund the docket, enforce the detainers and make DHS report every criminal alien it releases."

The brief also finds that the best available state-level data set, from Texas, is contested between researchers, and argues that Congress should settle the question with a mandatory, standardized federal data set.

Brief No. 14, the data appendix and a Hill fact sheet are available on the FSI website.

**The Founders' Square Institute** is a Washington, D.C., public-policy think tank.
